title: Understanding Thought-Action Fusion
summary: Why an intrusive thought is not a confession, and how clinicians can help clients separate thinking from doing.
body:
Thought-action fusion is the belief that having a thought about an event makes that event more likely, or is morally equivalent to acting on it. Clients experiencing intrusive harm-related thoughts often carry a private conviction that the thought itself is dangerous.

The clinical task is rarely to argue the thought away. It is to help the client notice the leap between "I had this thought" and "this thought means something about me" — and to sit with that gap long enough to see it clearly.

Over time, most clients discover that the thought's intensity was never evidence of its truth. It was evidence of how much they cared about not causing harm.

title: What Makes a Formulation Premature
summary: A short guide to slowing down before labeling avoidance as resistance.
body:
Calling a client "resistant" is often the fastest way to stop understanding them. Avoidance can be fear, shame, exhaustion, dissociation, or a dozen other things wearing the same outward shape.

A formulation becomes premature when a label arrives before the full picture does. The discipline is to keep asking what the avoidance is protecting, before deciding what to call it.

title: Reading the Metaworry Loop
summary: Distinguishing everyday worry from worry about worrying, and why the distinction changes treatment.
body:
Wells' metacognitive model separates Type 1 worry — worry about external events or bodily states — from Type 2 worry, which is worry about the act of worrying itself.

Clients stuck in a Type 2 loop often believe their worry is uncontrollable or dangerous in its own right. Naming that loop explicitly is frequently the first moment a client can step outside it, rather than inside it.
